evidence_set: Table 4 estimates the percentage of people using other illicit drugs by age 29 who had not already used cannabis when other-drug use began; this includes people who never used cannabis, not just those who later used it. The country-specific weighted cumulative estimates in its Total column are USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, Japan 83.2% and Nigeria 77.8%. The corresponding displayed n entries for other-drug use in Table 2 and not-already-cannabis histories in Table 4 are 16/13 in Japan and 8/7 in Nigeria. The supplied text does not explicitly define these n entries as unweighted observed counts; Table 4 labels its estimates projected, and Table 2 also notes projection for younger respondents. The reported percentages should therefore not be reconstructed as simple fractions of the displayed n entries. South Africa has 59.2% and Mexico 48.4%; the authors describe South Africa’s cannabis prevalence of 8.5% as moderate relative to the cross-country median of 9.8%. Thus not-cannabis-first histories also occur where cannabis use is moderate. Correspondence across countries is descriptive and does not establish prevalence as a cause of initiation order; the limitations warn that prevalence does not necessarily map to supply, demand or attitudes.

The review asserts that the true cannabis–other-drug association is negligible when the frequency of cannabis use in the population is taken into account, attributing that assertion to Earleywine 2002 rather than presenting a new analysis of it. This refers to population prevalence, not control for individual consumption frequency. It cites biometrical genetic/twin and genetic-correlation studies, including Kendler 2003/2007 and Agrawal 2004. No discussion of discordant co-twin-control studies such as Lynskey 2003 was identified in the complete captured article body or available references; however, the supplied saved text is truncated partway through the V references and does not permit certification of the complete reference list. The Conclusions describe common liability as parsimonious and empirically proven and say that the gateway hypothesis appears redundant. No systematic search or appraisal is described. Its Japan example pairs the pooled age-at-interview Total estimate of 83.2% not-already-cannabis histories with cannabis and other-drug prevalences for 18–29-year-olds; these have different age denominators.

evidence_set: The review’s imaging section reports mixed cognitive findings, including null behavioural comparisons and large differences on standardized tests outside the scanner, then states that polysubstance abuse is clearly associated with deficits in brain function and cognition while acknowledging difficulties in specifying relationships because of methodological differences, the substances used and possibly limited statistical power. Its Conclusion states elevated psychiatric and health risk and more pervasive cognitive deficits that place users at elevated risk of poorer treatment outcomes, and judges prevention and treatment approaches underdeveloped. These broad conclusions warrant caution in light of the mixed findings summarized here (editorial appraisal). The review does not describe a systematic search or formal appraisal and does not supply a count of cross-sectional versus prospective designs; it should not be treated as proving unsystematic selection or a particular design distribution. This appraisal is not a claim that all cited cognitive results were null.

The review says some earlier investigations did not capture parallel use of other drugs, and many studies used poorly matched controls. It does not characterize the missing other-drug data as occurring often. Findings may reflect pre-existing traits, drug use in general or associated lifestyle. The authors propose prospective work beginning with large cohorts of young people who are not or not yet users and may belong to specific risk groups, followed and re-examined over years with recorded drug histories and repeated tests of psychological functions and cognitive performance.
